newsitem.title: FINLAND: Yeltsin, Clinton get down to tough talks on NATO.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, Clinton get down to tough talks on NATO.

text.p: U.S. and Russian presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin tackle the problem of NATO enlargement on Friday, with little prospect they can reach agreement on the biggest question facing European security.

After a convivial dinner on Thursday in the Finnish capital, the two leaders meet for a day of what could be gruelling talks in a secluded modern villa, the official residence of Finnish President Martti Ahtisaari.
Surrounded by pine trees and built on granite, the house -- named Mantyniemi -- overlooks the Baltic Sea.

Moscow bitterly opposes NATO's plans to take in former Soviet-bloc states in Eastern Europe, saying it would isolate and threaten Russia. Washington says NATO will take in new members on schedule and that everyone will benefit as a result.

U.S. officials said the two presidents -- Clinton wheelchair-bound because of a leg injury, Yeltsin still recovering from long illness -- would probably tackle the NATO question soon after they start talks at 0800 GMT.
Clinton arrived first at the villa, driven there in a specially converted white van, and was greeted flanked by his advisers in briliant sunshine by Ahtisaari.

Western help for Russia's troubled transition to a market economy and possible deeper cuts in nuclear weapons are also on the agenda. If they can reach agreement, the two sides are expected to issue statements at the end of the summit.

Despite the jovial tone struck at Thursday's informal dinner, agreement will not be easy once the real business starts -- even though both Clinton and Yeltsin have faith in their post-Cold War partnership and say compromise can be found.
Yeltsin is under serious pressure from his nationalist and communist critics at home who accuse him of selling out to the West from their stronghold in the Russian parliament (Duma).
To make sure the 66-year-old Kremlin chief gets the point and fights Russia's corner, the Duma planned a debate on NATO on Friday which was expected to have a strident anti-Western tone.
Clinton, too, is under pressure on NATO enlargement.
An alliance summit in July is expected to invite Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to start membership talks. The new members would not join until 1999 at the earliest.

But those countries, and others in Europe, are watching closely to see there is no backsliding, nor secret deals cut with Moscow over the future of Europe -- as there was in 1945, at the end of World War Two.

The challenge for Clinton is to somehow convince Russia, particularly with economic help, that the West is a partner rather than an enemy and that an enlarged NATO means increased security for all in Europe rather than an increased threat.

U.S. officials said they would also press Russia at the summit to ratify within the next few weeks a long-delayed 1993 arms agreement cutting long-range nuclear missiles, perhaps with the help of additional concessions from Washington.
Breaking the logjam on arms control would be significant, with signs that the trust between Moscow and Washington which brought huge cuts in nuclear arsenals in the last few years is breaking down.

Yeltsin has just reshuffled his government to bring in more reformers and has drawn lavish praise from Washington on this. There is likely to be more Western help on offer to support Russia as it tackles organised crime and economic reforms, particularly since Yeltsin has pleased Washington by his clear commitment to change.
